mcqs.question: Why doesn't every call to malloc() trigger a system call into the kernel?
options: Because the userspace allocator requests memory from the OS in large batches and subdivides it internally, serving most malloc calls from that pool
Because malloc() is implemented entirely inside the CPU's MMU hardware
Because the kernel pre-allocates all memory a process will ever need at startup
Because malloc() only works for allocations smaller than one page
mcqs.explanation: The allocator amortizes kernel round-trips by requesting memory in bulk and handing out smaller pieces from that pool without a syscall each time. There's no MMU-hardware implementation of malloc, no full upfront pre-allocation, and malloc works for allocations of any size, small or large.

mcqs.question: Why might an allocator use mmap for a very large allocation instead of extending the heap with sbrk?
options: mmap allocations execute faster per byte than sbrk allocations
sbrk cannot allocate more than 4 KB at a time
An mmap-backed region can be returned to the OS immediately on free via munmap, rather than sitting in the heap's free list waiting to be reused
mmap is required for any allocation larger than one page by the C standard
mcqs.explanation: mmap-backed large allocations can be handed straight back to the OS on free, avoiding permanent heap growth for one-off big requests — that's the practical reason allocators route large requests there. Per-byte speed isn't the driver, sbrk has no 4 KB cap, and there's no such C-standard mandate.

mcqs.question: What advantage do segregated free lists (one list per size class) give an allocator over a single first-fit free list?
options: They eliminate internal fragmentation completely
They remove the need for chunk headers entirely
They make allocation faster by pulling directly from the matching size-class list instead of scanning for a fit
They guarantee no memory is ever returned to the OS
mcqs.explanation: Segregated free lists let a request round up to its size class and pull straight from that class's list — roughly O(1) instead of scanning. They don't eliminate internal fragmentation (rounding up to a class still wastes some space), don't remove headers, and don't affect whether memory is returned to the OS.

mcqs.question: In the buddy allocation algorithm, what happens when a freed block's buddy is also free?
options: Nothing — buddies are only checked when a new allocation request arrives
The allocator immediately requests more memory from the OS
The freed block is discarded and unavailable for future allocations
The two buddies merge back into the larger block they were originally split from, and this merge can cascade upward
mcqs.explanation: The defining feature of the buddy system is that it checks and merges free buddies immediately on free, cascading upward if the merged block's buddy is also free — this is what keeps fragmentation bounded. It doesn't wait for a new request, discard the block, or need to ask the OS for more memory to do this.

mcqs.question: A program calls free() on the same pointer twice. What's the dangerous consequence?
options: The program crashes immediately and safely every time
The chunk ends up on the free list twice, so a future allocation can hand out the same memory to two different callers simultaneously
The OS detects the mistake and blocks the second call automatically
Nothing — the second call is silently ignored by the allocator's design
mcqs.explanation: A double-free corrupts the allocator's own bookkeeping by inserting the same chunk into the free list twice, which can later let two live pointers alias the same memory — a serious bug and a known exploit primitive. It isn't guaranteed to crash safely, isn't blocked by the OS, and isn't silently harmless.

mcqs.question: A long-running server's memory usage grows steadily over days even though no single allocation looks unusually large. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The operating system is failing to reclaim freed memory
A memory leak — the program keeps allocating memory and losing every pointer that could reach it, so it's never freed
This can only be explained by a kernel bug
The CPU cache is filling up with allocated objects
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic leak signature: reachable pointers are lost over time (not overwritten references, never-cleared containers) while the memory stays allocated and valid. The OS reclaims all process memory on exit without exception, so it isn't an OS or kernel failure, and the CPU cache has nothing to do with heap allocation lifetimes.
